fields.Text: Data: known facts that can be {{c1::recorded}} and have an {{c2::implicit meaning}}.
A database is a collection of {{c1::related data}}.

fields.Back: The part of the real world about which data is stored in a database; a database is a model of a mini-world. Examples: a medical office, a retail business, a library.
A software package/system to facilitate the creation and maintenance of a computerized database.
The DBMS software together with the data itself (sometimes the applications are included too).

fields.Text: A DBMS is the {{c1::software}}; a database is the {{c1::data}}; a database system is {{c2::the DBMS together with the data}} (sometimes plus the applications).

fields.Front: What is a flat file? What is a record?
fields.Back: A flat file is a plain file ('really just a TXT or ASCII file') where each line/block holds one record; a record (also called an instance, like one object of a class) is one occurrence of the kind of thing the file stores, made of a fixed set of fields.

fields.Front: In a flat file of customer lines, identify: a piece of data, a record, the flat file.
fields.Back: A single field value (e.g. a phone number) is data; one customer's line is a record; the whole file is the flat file.

fields.Front: Video 1 opens with a grocery list, a letter, a spreadsheet of grades, a student list and an Access file, and asks which are databases. What is the instructor's answer?
fields.Back: All of them: a database is 'just a group of related data'. It does not have to live in Access, MySQL or any DBMS.

fields.Text: The instructor's example of a mini-world: within Western, a database just for the {{c1::Computer Science department}}; she calls narrowing the world this way '{{c2::divide and conquer}}'.

fields.Front: In the flat-file row '251012345,Homer,Simpson,CS', how many pieces of data are there, and why is the single digit '2' not a piece of data?
fields.Back: Four (student number, first name, last name, department). A single character has no inherent meaning; it is the nine characters together that mean a student number.

fields.Text: A flat file is 'really just a {{c1::TXT (ASCII)}} file'; each row is a {{c2::record}}, which you can think of as an {{c3::instance}} of a class.

fields.Front: Describe the loop the instructor wrote in first year to read a flat file.
fields.Back: While not at the end of the line: read until a comma, read until the next comma, ... to the end of the line; put the values into variables or a record; go to the next line and repeat until end of file. Writing was the mirror image: value, comma, value, comma, newline.

fields.Front: In the flat-file world, what did the instructor call a 'database'?
fields.Back: A group of related flat files together (e.g. a students file and a departments file) that keep the organisation's data.

fields.Front: List the four learning objectives of Video 1 (Introduction).
fields.Back: Define data, database, mini-world and DBMS; know what a flat file looks like; find a piece of data and a record within a flat file; give at least three reasons to prefer a DBMS over flat files.

fields.Front: What lesson does the instructor draw from the student list whose last column turned out to look like a date rather than a student number?
fields.Back: You have to know the context of the data to know what it means.
